senses: a corner; a part; a secluded place
曲.shuowen: 象器曲受物之形。或說曲，蠶薄也。
曲.shuowenEn: It shows the form of a vessel, curved, that receives things. Some say 曲 is a silkworm tray.
曲.story: A single picture: a curved container. From “bent” come a river’s turn, a corner, a twisted meaning, and a melody. The Laozi opens passage 22 with an old proverb, 曲則全, “bent, then whole”, and closes by asking whether the ancients spoke empty words. Passage 45 has the partner line: 大直若屈, “great straightness seems bent”.
曲.gap: “Yield” in English is a decision. 曲 is a shape. Legge’s “partial” takes another real sense of the word, a corner or fragment, and loses the curve.

senses: to strike; to attack a state
伐.shuowen: 擊也。从人持戈。一曰敗也。
伐.shuowenEn: To strike. A person who holds a dagger-axe. Another sense: to ruin.
伐.story: A person and a halberd. The word for a campaign against a state became a word for bragging: to attack with one’s own merits. The Laozi uses that sense three times: not self-praising, so there is merit (22); the self-praiser has no merit (24); achieve the result and do not boast (30).
伐.gap: English “boast” is only vain. 伐 keeps the violence: self-praise as an assault on the listener.

全.story: The Shuowen glosses the word “complete”; it is commonly added that the form with jade stood for a piece of jade with no flaw. In the Warring States it was a word of survival and of strategy: to keep one’s life whole, to take a state whole. The proverb of passage 22 says the bent is what stays 全. Our text of passage 16 has it in the great chain: even-handed, then whole; whole, then heaven.
全.gap: “Perfect” and “complete” add an ideal. 全 only says that no piece has been broken off.
全.shuowenEn: Complete. From 入 and 工. (The Shuowen enters the word under the older graph 仝.)

枉.shuowenEn: Slanting and bent. From 木 (wood), with 㞷 for the sound.
枉.story: A carpenter’s word for a board that is not true, and then a judge’s word for a crooked verdict and its victim. The proverb in passage 22 says: crooked, then straight. A saying of the diplomats, which Mencius rejected, promised more: bend a foot and straighten eight.
枉.gap: English “crooked” blames; “wronged” pities. 枉 is both the bent thing and the one bent.

senses: (first sense) to cut firewood: later 薪
新.shuowenEn: To get wood. From 斤 (axe), with the left part for the sound.

parts.m: left part: sound (a tree with 辛)

新.story: At first the word for felling and splitting wood. The sense “new” took over the graph, and firewood was given a grass top: 薪. The Laozi pairs it with 敝, worn out: worn, then new (22).
新.gap: “New” in English is abstract. The graph still has the axe and the white of fresh-cut wood.

senses: a pattern, a standard, a model
a rule, a form; a ceremony
式.shuowenEn: A standard. From 工 (the carpenter’s square), with 弋 for the sound.
式.story: The pattern piece from which others are cut. The sage holds the One and is the 式 of the world (22); know the white, keep the black, and be the 式 of the world (28); to know the two models of rule is a standing 式 (65). The Mawangdui silk texts read 牧, herdsman, in passage 22.
式.gap: “Model” in English suggests a person to imitate. 式 is nearer to a gauge: it does nothing, and things are checked against it.

senses: to pity; to be careful of
矜.shuowenEn: The shaft of a spear. From 矛 (spear), with 今 for the sound.
矜.story: A spear-shaft, held upright; and so, of a person, stiff with self-regard. Not self-proud, so lasting (22); the self-proud does not last (24); achieve the result and do not be proud (30).
矜.gap: One graph for “proud” and “to pity”. English has no word that looks down in both ways.

senses: to pull against; to contend, to fight over
爭.shuowenEn: To pull. From 𠬪 (two hands) and 𠂆.
爭.story: Two hands that pull at one thing. 不爭, “no contending”, is one of the book’s signatures: do not honour the worthy and the people will not contend (3); water benefits all and does not contend (8); because of no contending, no one can contend with such a one (22, 66); the power of not-contending (68); heaven’s way does not contend and is good at winning (73); the sage’s way is to act and not contend (81).
爭.gap: “Not striving” sounds lazy and “not competing” sounds meek. 不爭 is to let go of the rope.

senses: to fit, to be at ease with
得.shuowenEn: To walk and come upon something. From 彳 (a step), with 㝵 for the sound.

parts.m: a hand on a cowrie: to get

得.story: A hand closes on a shell, on the road. The word sounds like 德, inner power, and early writers defined the one by the other: 德 is what one has got. The Laozi plays on the pair in passage 23. It warns against 難得之貨, goods hard to get (3, 12, 64), and says: few, then gain (22).
得.gap: English keeps “get” and “virtue” far apart. In Chinese they are near-homophones, and thinkers used the echo.
